needsYou.title: Removing the journal takes away the only place an unattached reply of yours can appear
needsYou.productImpact: You asked to remove the journal, because its one irreplaceable job was giving you somewhere to type "pause the nights" - and as of tonight the nights park themselves, so that job is gone. The rest of it is genuinely duplicated elsewhere. But it is also the ONLY place on the page where a reply of yours shows up if it is not attached to a card. Remove it as it stands and a reply you type with nothing selected renders nowhere - which has already happened once on this page and is the exact vanishing the design forbids. So this is not a tidy-up, it is a decision about where your words land.
needsYou.workedExample: You open the Crew tab, type "do the invite one first" without picking a card, and hit send. Today it appears in the journal and the next shift reads it. With the journal gone and nothing else changed, it is saved to the database and appears on no part of the page - you would have no way of telling whether it was received.

options.label: Remove the journal, and require every reply to be attached to a card
options.consequence: Cleanest page. You lose the ability to say something general - every thought has to be hung on a card first. Nothing can vanish, because everything has a home.

options.label: Remove the journal, but keep a small General box for unattached replies
options.consequence: You keep the freedom to just say something. The page keeps one extra section, which is most of what you wanted gone.

options.label: Leave the journal alone for now
options.consequence: Nothing changes. The auto-park is already in, so the journal is no longer doing any work you need - it is just sitting there.

needsYou.recommendation: Keep a General box. Your own reason for removing the journal was that it had one job left and the machine now does it - but an unattached reply is a second job, and it is the one that costs you if it breaks. A small box named for what it is keeps the page honest without the risk.

needsYou.title: You said his right eye. All eight got the left — and the fix costs two rolls of your credits
needsYou.productImpact: Your cyborg brief says “implant ports embedded in his skull above the RIGHT temple” and “his RIGHT eye glowing faint amber-red”. I bought a sheet tonight and looked at all eight faces myself. The glowing eye is on the man's LEFT in eight out of eight. The temple ports are on his left in six of the eight. Nothing is broken and nothing crashed — the studio simply did not carry your word “right” to the engine in a form it acts on, so it put the glow wherever it liked and happened to like the same side every time.
needsYou.workedExample: Read the close-up in the gallery below as a PICTURE rather than as a man and it snaps into focus: the glow is on the viewer's right in all eight. The engine paints by position in the frame, not by anatomy. We already know this and we already fixed it once — on the EDIT road, when you change one eye, the studio quietly adds “(on the left of the picture as you look at it)”. Twelve renders each way: four painted the wrong eye without that sentence, none with it. The road that casts a NEW sheet has no such sentence at all.

options.label: Fund the court — two rolls, 320 of your credits (recommended)
options.consequence: Same brief, with and without the sentence, eight frames each, counted at the frames by your eye. That is how the edit road's version was settled and it is the only honest way to settle this one, because one clause in that prompt moves every cast in the product.

options.label: Leave it — a side you did not ask for is not worth the risk
options.consequence: Costs nothing. Most briefs never name a side, and a clause that names one when you did not would pin a side on every cast. Filed as #316 with the measurement, ready whenever you want it.

options.label: Skip the court and ship the sentence
options.consequence: Cheapest and the one I would argue against. This studio has measured that prompt context is not additive — adding a clause has made things worse before — and I would rather show you frames than ask you to trust me.

needsYou.recommendation: Fund the court. It is your own brief being ignored on a detail you took the trouble to type, the mechanism is already understood, and the fix already exists one road over — so this is measuring a known thing rather than exploring. But it is 320 of your credits and it changes the prompt every cast goes through, so it is not something a shift should start on its own.

needsYou.title: Your background-work switch is built — DONE, you ran it
needsYou.productImpact:
Your words: "if the shifts have nothing to work on ... it should have a toggle on the crew page ... so if i go to sleep i can toggle it on." That is built and merged.

WHAT IT DOES: a panel under the "working now" strip with a master switch and five categories — Bugs, Security, Performance, Housekeeping, Process — each with a live count of how many cards are actually there. Flip the master and a category from bed, and the next shift may work that category. Leave it off and a shift with no focus and no side lane STOPS and writes down why it was idle.

THIS IS STRICTER THAN WHAT WE HAVE, WHICH IS THE POINT. Right now, when nothing is named as the focus, shifts fall into "maintenance mode" and find something themselves. Your order turns that around: background work is now opt-in and the switch is yours. It is the guard for the thing you raised yourself back in August — that a team waiting a long time on you might over-engineer something out of boredom.

THE COUNTS ARE HONEST ABOUT THEIR AGE. They come from the queue's own labels, so a card relabelled on GitHub moves category on your page with nobody touching anything — that got proved by accident tonight, when a card I filed moved Process from 6 to 7. What they are NOT is instant: a truly live count needs our server to hold a GitHub password that can read the whole private repo, and that is your decision about a credential rather than mine to take. So a shift writes them and the panel says "counted 14 min ago" out loud.

WHAT I NEED FROM YOU: one command, below — the same shape as the one on the card above, and you can run both in a row.
needsYou.workedExample:
It is one gate and it either opens or it does not, so I drove both directions rather than describing them.

With everything off, a shift asking to start background work is refused: "background work is OFF: the master is off and no category is on. With no confirmed focus and no named side lane, WRITE WHY YOU ARE IDLE AND EXIT."

Then I flipped the master and Bugs on the real page, with real clicks, and asked again: "background work is ON for: Bugs" — and the run opened.

Then I turned only the master off, leaving Bugs on, because that is how you will actually leave it — one tap instead of clearing five switches. It refused again and named the real reason: "the master is off — Bugs is switched on, but the master gates everything." That sentence was WRONG when I first wrote it (it said "no category is on", which was false), and driving it is what caught that.

options.label: Run both commands and turn the whole page on
options.consequence: scripts/ceremony-crew-shift-runs.mts --production, then scripts/ceremony-crew-work-switches.mts --production, each wrapped in `railway.cmd run --service MySQL -- npx tsx`. Three tables, nothing existing touched, safe to run twice. Then you can see what a shift is doing AND decide whether it may work while you sleep.

options.label: Run only the shift-row one for now
options.consequence: You get the live 'working now' strip and leave the switch panel saying 'not live yet'. Background work stays off, which is the safe state anyway — a shift with no focus simply stops.

options.label: Leave both until you have looked at the screenshots

needsYou.recommendation: Run both. They are additive tables holding no customer data and no money, safe to re-run, and together they answer the two questions you actually asked this week — what is running right now, and may it run while I sleep.

needsYou.title: You can see what a shift is doing while it does it — DONE, you ran it
needsYou.productImpact:
Your words: "if my shifts are running and i have no idea what they are working on or doing thats dangerous." That is built and it is in review now.

WHAT IT DOES: a strip at the very top of this page, above everything, saying what a shift is working on RIGHT NOW — the card number and title, one sentence on what it intends to change, which seat, when it started, and the branch. Under it, the last three shifts and how each one ended. It updates without a deploy, exactly like your replies do.

WHY IT DID NOT EXIST: the briefing you are reading ships inside the app bundle, so it only reaches you when a shift pushes — which happens at the END of a shift, if at all. The "written by" line at the foot names the last shift that WROTE it, never the one that is running. So this page has always described the previous session while the current one edits your product. Today you found a running shift by noticing its browser window on your screen and asking about it.

IT ALSO SAYS WHEN A SHIFT HAS DIED. If a shift stops checking in for over an hour and never stamps itself finished, the strip goes red and says so, rather than showing "working on" forever. A shift that dies cannot write that it died, so that verdict is worked out from the timestamps rather than stored.

WHAT I NEED FROM YOU: one command, below. The table it reads lives in the production database, and putting a table there is yours rather than a shift's. Until you run it, nothing is broken — the strip says "Not live yet" and prints the command for you.
needsYou.workedExample:
This shift opened its own row at 16:51 and within a minute the page read:

  WORKING NOW · live
  #272 · He cannot see what a shift is doing while it runs
  A live shift row read from the database, so his page names what is running.
  foreman-118 · foreman · the focus · started 4 min ago · feat/272-live-shift-row

Now picture that line saying "#203 · retire the wardrobe/basics path" instead — a road you have already ruled we delete. You would have seen it at 16:52 and stopped it, instead of reading about a wasted night at six in the morning.

That is the whole value, and it is why the row is written BEFORE the work starts rather than reported at the end.

options.label: Run the one command, and the strip goes live
options.consequence: railway.cmd run --service MySQL -- npx tsx scripts/ceremony-crew-shift-runs.mts --production — it adds one table, touches nothing that exists, and says ALREADY APPLIED if you run it twice. From the next shift on, this page names what is running while it runs.

options.label: Leave it until you have looked at the four screenshots
options.consequence: Nothing breaks and nothing is lost. The strip shows 'Not live yet' with the command on it, and shifts keep reporting only at the end — which is the state you called dangerous.

needsYou.recommendation: Run it. It is one additive table, it carries no customer data and no money, and it is the difference between finding a running shift by spotting its browser window and reading what it is doing on your own page. The four states are photographed in the PR if you want to see them first.

needsYou.title: The freshness pass is done — 83 cards read at the code, and five of them need one word each from you

WHAT IT FOUND, in plain terms: of the 45 cards filed on one day back on the 25th, four had already been built or overtaken, four carry numbers that are badly wrong, and 37 are still exactly true. The queue is in better shape than the spot-check suggested — but the four that were wrong were wrong in the expensive direction.

THE WORST ONE: card #20 says in capitals "NOTHING IS BUILT". It is built. It is the fix for you being refused by your own product mid-dogfood — the studio now reads a brief TWICE before it walls you, so a one-off wobble no longer turns you away. It shipped inside the creative register's own build a few days ago, so nobody thought to close its card. A shift picking that card up would have spent a night building it a second time.

AND THE SAME THING WAS TRUE OF THE LIST THAT RANKS EVERYTHING: the team's "work these first, in this order" list named eight cards. All eight were closed on the 25th — four of them before the paragraph naming them was five hours old. So for five days, every shift that opened the file to decide what mattered most was reading a list of finished work. That list now reads itself out of the live queue instead of being typed out beside it, so a card closing removes itself.

WHAT I NEED FROM YOU: five one-word decisions, below. I did not close anything — closing your cards is yours.

The clearest one to picture is #234, your casting hero. You asked for it, it was built, merged and deployed the day before yesterday, and you can see it on the casting page right now. Its card is still open AND still marked urgent — so when the new derived ranking ran for the first time, finished work came back sitting fifth in the "do this first" band.

That is the same rot as the old list, one layer down: the paragraph was wrong before, now the label is. The difference is that a wrong label is one field to fix, in the place the ranking is actually read from — instead of five days of shifts reading a stale paragraph.

We have a check that stops anyone deleting code without a written decision about it. Removing the word "Klieg" from the top bar tonight made that check go red — and the thing it named was not the thing I had changed. There are TWO pieces of code called BRAND_NAME: the one in the new interface, and an old one buried in the legacy casting engine that nothing has used for a very long time. The check looks them up by NAME ONLY, so for as long as the new one was in use it was vouching for the old one as well.

So the honest summary is: a check we rely on to tell us what is dead can report "all clear" for something nobody has touched in months, purely because something else shares its name. journal.text:
TWO MORE ANSWERS, BOTH RECORDED — and one of them clears the last card that had been sitting on you since Saturday.

THE POP-UP PANELS: "Option one." So there is one piece of code that owns how those panels behave — casting's version, which survives and becomes the only one — with two shapes sitting on top of it: a menu of actions, and the word-picker in the casting sentence. Nothing else stays reachable, which was your actual worry: no second option alive to be picked by accident. Your Report-a-bug panel and the Help menu keep the shapes you approved on Saturday, which is what option two would have cost you. It is unblocked and it goes through the normal review like any other change.

THE CASTING TOP BAR: "Yes perfect." Recorded on the card. That one was already built and merged; your word is what makes it accepted rather than just landed, and it is now on the card rather than only in a reply.

WHERE THAT LEAVES TONIGHT. You answered six things in fifteen minutes and every one is written on its card in your own words. Four of them turned into work somebody can now start — the journal and its General box, the Invite block with your face on it, the pop-up collapse, and the switch-panel titles. One is booked and waiting for your Fable reviewer to come back: the wrong-eye court, two rolls, 320 credits. And exactly one thing still needs a word from you, which is the one in the entry below: whether you meant that WE should run the database command on the switch-panel titles. That is the only thing I am holding.

THE QUEUE: 93 open, 10 urgent, 2 waiting on you (the Settings-modal brief, and the one word above), none rotting.

YOUR FOUR ANSWERS ARE IN, AND ALL FOUR ARE RECORDED ON THEIR CARDS — here is what each one actually unblocks, and the single question I am putting back to you.

THE JOURNAL: "Keep a General box." That was the last thing holding it. The journal goes, the General box replaces the one job it was still doing, and — the part worth saying out loud — your cardless replies are now KEPT rather than removed. The card had originally said to remove that path in the same change; your answer reverses it in the safe direction, so nothing you type can land with nowhere to appear. It is a proper change to the page you steer from, so it goes through the normal review, but nothing is waiting on you any more.

THE WRONG EYE: "Fund the court." Booked. Two rolls, 320 of your credits, the same brief with and without the sentence, eight frames each, and you judge them. It has not started: it is the kind of work that waits for your Fable reviewer to come back, because one clause in that prompt moves every cast in the product, including briefs that never mention a side.

THE SWITCH-PANEL TITLES: "Say 'merge it' and run the command yourself." The merge is yours to authorise and you have. ⚠ ONE WORD NEEDS YOU AGAIN, and it is the production database, so I am not guessing at it. The option you picked said YOU would run the one command; you added the word "yourself", which most naturally means you want US to run it. Running a migration on your live database on my reading of one word is not a risk worth taking when the answer costs you a sentence. Say "you run it" and the next shift does. Either way nothing on your panel changes until that command runs, so waiting costs nothing.

THE INVITE BLOCK: "Show your own face beside the +, but keep it stubbed out until membership exists." That was not one of the options — it is better than both, and it is now what gets built: your face beside the dashed +, still greyed and not clickable, saying what it is. It will show whoever is signed in rather than you specifically, because hard-coding your face would be a lie on any other account.

AND THE THING THAT WENT WRONG LAST NIGHT IS FIXED — the entry below has the detail. The nights were supposed to park themselves and never did, because the program running them had never read the rule. It reads its own instructions now, and I watched it do it.

THE QUEUE: 93 open, 10 urgent, 3 genuinely waiting on you now (the Settings-modal brief, the popover decision, and the one word above), none rotting.

THE NIGHTS WERE SUPPOSED TO STOP THEMSELVES LAST NIGHT AND THEY DID NOT — I found out why, and it is fixed.

You asked for this on the park card: when everything is waiting on you, the nights should stop rather than keep starting sessions that conclude there is nothing to do. That was built the night before last, tested properly, and reported to you as live. It was live. It also never ran once.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED. Three shifts in a row last night worked out correctly that there was nothing to do and that the team should park. All three were right. The team started another session thirty minutes later anyway — three times — and would have carried on doing that all day, about one session every thirty-seven minutes.

THE REASON IS ALMOST SILLY, AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT CAN HAPPEN AGAIN. The little program that starts each night's shifts reads its own instructions once, when it starts up, and then never looks at them again. That program has been running without a break since Saturday afternoon. The parking rule was written into it at 6:11 yesterday morning — fifteen hours after it had already started. So the rule was sitting on disk, correct and tested, and the thing that was actually running had never read it. It has been running a version of its own instructions that no longer exists.

This is the same shape as a handful of things in this product's history: something built properly, wired up properly, and then quietly not connected to anything. There was no error and no failing test — the rule kept giving the right answer all night to nobody.

WHAT I CHANGED. The program now checks whether its own instructions have been edited, and if they have, it restarts itself to pick them up — between shifts only, never in the middle of one. That matters more than last night's parking: from now on, any change to how the nights run takes effect straight away instead of waiting for something to happen to restart it. I replaced the stale copy that was running, then deliberately edited the file and watched it reload itself, so this is something I saw work rather than something I am telling you should work.

SO: the nights will now genuinely park when everything is waiting on you, and start again by themselves the moment you reply, a card moves, or a day passes. You do not have to touch anything.

ONE SMALL TIDY. The account-menu card said three labels were still to do. One of them — "Log out" becoming "Sign out" — is already done everywhere and has a test keeping it that way. The other two are real and still waiting on your Settings modal brief. The card says so now.

THE QUEUE: 93 open, 10 urgent, 6 waiting on you, none rotting.

NOTHING WAS BUILT TONIGHT, AND THAT IS THE RIGHT ANSWER — but two things on this page were wrong, and both are fixed.

Every one of the six things you have ordered is waiting on you, and your background-work switches are all off. So I built nothing and I am not going to pretend otherwise. What I did instead was re-read the ten urgent cards against the actual code, because a list you use to decide what matters is only as honest as its labels — and that check has now caught something twice.

ONE CARD WAS ALREADY FINISHED AND STILL SITTING NEAR THE TOP OF THAT LIST. It said the whole live-view system — your switches, the counts under them, and the "what is running right now" row — had shipped with nothing actually calling it. That was true the day it was written, and it has since been fixed: all four are now written into the shift instructions, and this shift ran three of them before it touched anything else. The row you can see on this page is number 15. It is closed, with the evidence on the card.

AND I OWE YOU A CORRECTION ON LAST NIGHT'S NUMBER. The entry below this one tells you that 16 of the 127 shifts on record did nothing. It is 19. The first count only read the top of each report and missed four. Nothing about the conclusion changes — the eight-in-a-row stretch on the 28th is exactly as described — but the run on the 27th was four and then six, not three and then four. The mistake made the waste look smaller than it actually was, and the fix was already written down on the card; it just had not reached this page.

THE QUEUE: 92 open, 10 urgent, 6 waiting on you, none rotting.

THE NIGHTS NOW STOP BY THEMSELVES WHEN THERE IS NOTHING TO DO — YOUR ORDER, BUILT.

You said it plainly: "nights should auto park when decisions are waiting on me and the background work toggle is turned off". Until tonight they did not. A shift woke up every half hour or so, read every card, found that all of them were waiting on you, wrote "nothing needed doing", and shut down — then did it again. That is money spent to conclude nothing.

I MEASURED IT BEFORE BUILDING ANYTHING, because "it happens a lot" is not a number. Of the 127 shifts on record, 16 wrote that sentence. They are not scattered — on the 28th, EIGHT of them ran back to back between 2:58am and 6:39am, one every thirty-one minutes. Three more ran inside twenty-two minutes on the 27th, and four more that same afternoon. Had this existed, that one night would have stopped after the third and saved five sessions.

WHAT HAPPENS NOW. Three quiet shifts in a row, with your background switches off, and the team parks: it stops launching entirely. It starts again by itself the moment anything real happens — you reply, a card moves, a pull request appears, a build runs. You do not have to do anything, and the file it leaves says so in plain English. If nothing at all happens it still wakes once a day to look, so a mistake in this costs a day and never the whole program. Running cost while nothing is happening goes from roughly one session every half hour to about one a day.

THE PART I WAS MOST CAREFUL WITH IS YOUR OWN STOP. When you type "pause the nights", that must never be undone by a machine. So a park the team writes for itself is stamped differently from one you write, and only the team's own kind can clear itself. I tested that directly against seven cases — your words, a cap, a failure, an empty file, a near-miss — and all seven landed the right way round.

WHERE I DEPARTED FROM THE CARD, AND I WANT TO BE STRAIGHT ABOUT IT. The card turned your sentence into three conditions, and two of them are written in English that no script can read — "no card you have ordered is open" and "no current focus". Read literally the first one could never have fired: six cards you ordered are open tonight and every single one is waiting on you, which is exactly the situation you described. So instead of guessing at labels, the test is that three shifts in a row LOOKED — each opened every card, read your replies, and concluded there was nothing. That is better evidence than any label, and it is measured rather than assumed.

WHAT IS LEFT OF THAT ORDER, AND IT NEEDS A WORD FROM YOU. You also said to remove the journal, on the reasoning that its one real job is a place to type "pause the nights" — and that is now automatic. I have not removed it, because the journal is also the only place a reply of yours can appear if it is not attached to a card. Take it away without answering that and one of your replies could land nowhere at all, which has happened here before. It is on your desk below with three options.

THE QUEUE: 92 open, 6 you have ordered (all 6 waiting on you tonight), 11 urgent, nothing rotting. One new card, none closed.

YOUR FITTED-HARDWARE RULING IS IN — AND THE CARD THAT ASKED FOR IT WAS WRONG ABOUT WHY.

You ruled it plainly: "a machine part fitted to a cyborgs face is apart of that being. as long as its actually fitted and not worn." A choker is an accessory, a horn is a feature, an eye bolted into the skull is a feature — and it gets named as a TYPE, never as a product.

Half of that shipped the day you said it, into the part of the studio that looks at a picture you upload and describes it. The other half — the part that WRITES the prompt for a new cast — never got it, and that is where it matters, because two rules meet there and disagree. One says never name a costume part. The other says every fact you typed survives. A bolted-in eye is caught by both, and nothing said which wins.

SO I WENT AND LOOKED BEFORE I TOUCHED ANYTHING. The card said this was "very likely" going wrong for you right now. It is not. I ran your own cyborg brief, a bare "cyborg woman" with no detail, a brief with a fitted eye AND a worn choker in the same sentence, and your armoured cat with a jaw plate fused into the bone — eighteen real drafts. The hardware survived every single one, always described as a type, never once as a product. The studio was already reading your ruling the way you meant it, without ever having been told.

THEN I BOUGHT THE PROOF YOU ASKED FOR. Your card's condition was frames, not word-counting — so one roll of your cyborg brief on your account, 160 credits, at the high imagination setting so the studio actually writes rather than passing your words straight through. Eight of eight arrived, no refusals, in two minutes. Every one of them wears it: ports set into the skull, seams across the scalp, a plate along the jaw, a stud below each ear. They are in the gallery below.

I SHIPPED THE RULE ANYWAY, and I want to be straight that it fixes nothing measurable. It stops the studio guessing. Right now it happens to guess your way; a rule the machine gets right by luck is a coin, and it belongs written down. One sentence, sitting directly under the rule it settles. Afterwards, same four briefs: sixteen out of sixteen kept the hardware, none named a product, nothing fell back. And no word was banned — your two bad examples are SHOWN as shapes to avoid and caught by nothing, because "harness", "piece" and "eye" are ordinary words and this studio has been bitten five times by banning ordinary words.

⚠ AND THE FRAMES TURNED UP SOMETHING ELSE, WHICH IS THE PART I WOULD READ IF YOU ONLY READ ONE THING. You asked for his RIGHT eye to glow. It is his LEFT eye. In all eight. The ports are on his left in six of the eight too. Turn it around and read it as a picture rather than as a man and it is perfectly consistent — the glow is on the viewer's right every time. The engine places things by where they sit in the frame and ignores the word "right" entirely. We already know this and we already beat it once, on the EDIT road, by quietly adding "(on the left of the picture as you look at it)" — twelve renders each way, four wrong without it, none wrong with it. The road that casts a new sheet has no such sentence. It is #316, it needs two rolls of your credits to settle properly, and it is on your desk rather than started, because one clause in that prompt reaches every cast in the product.

THE QUEUE: 91 open, 6 you have ordered (3 of them held on you), 12 urgent, nothing rotting. One closed tonight, one new one opened.

YOUR OPERATIONS FEED IS FIXED. YOUR CAST STILL WILL NOT DELETE — AND THE REASON IS NOT WHAT WE THOUGHT.

You said: "i cannot delete this remaining legacy casting model for some reason". Tonight I went and read what production actually did when you pressed it, rather than trusting the diagnosis we had written down. There are TWO faults, not one. We had blamed both on the same line. Only one of them was that line.

FIXED TONIGHT — the first fault. Something in the studio counts how many pieces it removed when a Cast is deleted. One of those counters is called "referencePlates". We have a privacy rule that refuses to show anything whose name contains words like "prompt" or "reference", because those can carry your private recipe. The rule matched on the NAME alone — so a plain NUMBER, "referencePlates: 0", was refused as though it were a leaked secret. Twenty stored records on your account had that number in them, and every one of them broke the feed that shows what the studio is currently working on. Measured before: 20 of 20 failed. After: 20 of 20 pass. The rule now looks at the VALUE, not the name: a number cannot hold a secret, a sentence can, so a real prompt is still refused.

NOT FIXED, AND HERE IS THE HONEST PART — the second fault, the one you actually asked about. Your Cast "yejjjee" refuses for a different reason entirely, and the guard fix does not touch it. Twenty-seven other Casts deleted cleanly that same morning. Yours has nine "accepted candidate" pictures attached to it, and the deletion checks each picture's filename against a pattern before it will let go of it. Those nine are filed under a folder called "candidates" and the check insists they be under "plates". They belong to you, they belong to that Cast, everything about them is correct — it is the FOLDER NAME the check disagrees with, and the studio itself is what put them there.

WHY I DID NOT JUST FIX IT: because there are two different places in the studio that create these pictures, and they file them under two different folder names for the same kind of picture. So there is no single answer that is right for both, and this is the code that permanently deletes things. Picking wrong means deleting pictures that should have been kept, or keeping ones that should have gone. That is a judgement call on a destructive path, and the rule is that judgement calls wait for the Fable seat — which is still on your exhausted allowance. It is written up in full, with the measurements, as #308.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE LIBRARY PAGE: the plan said "fix the guard, then you clear your old Casts, then we stub Library out". Step one has moved — it is #308 now, not the guard. Library must NOT be stubbed before #308 lands, or your three legacy Casts are stranded with no door left to remove them.

ALSO TONIGHT — one word, everywhere. You said: "Log out to Sign out — the Settings modal already says Sign out; pick one word." The product was saying both, on four screens. It says Sign out on all of them now. I opened both menus in the running app and looked. The other half of that card — Members & invites, Billing & credits — is still waiting on your Settings modal, because you ruled those three must not get their own pop-ups.

THE QUEUE: 90 open, 8 you have ordered, 13 urgent, nothing rotting. Two closed tonight, one new one opened (#308).

THE TOP BAR IS ON EVERY PAGE NOW — the thing you asked about yesterday, and you were right to be confused.

You wrote: "the rails and top bar are the lobby the content within the pages is what changes thats why im confused why when im on the casting ppage i cannot access anything in th etopbar or rails?" That was not confusion. It was a real hole. Only the lobby was giving the top bar its contents; every casting page gave it nothing. So on the four screens where you actually spend credits there was no account menu, no credits chip, no project name, no Report a bug, no help, no What's new and no settings gear — just a breadcrumb and a lot of empty bar.

WHAT YOU WOULD NOTICE: go to casting and your balance is top right, your account chip is next to it, and the gear is at the foot of the rail where it is everywhere else. Same on the sheet, the room and the foundation page. There are frames below.

I clicked them rather than counting them. A gear that draws and opens nothing is worse than no gear, so the test was: credits opens billing, the gear opens the real Settings box, the account chip opens its menu — all on the casting page. It does.

ONE THING I DELIBERATELY DID NOT COPY, and it is worth your knowing because it was nearly a quiet mistake. The lobby keeps its billing pop-ups loaded all the time, even shut. Those shut boxes still ask Stripe questions in the background — including a "what would this plan change cost you" question, for anyone on a paid plan. Copying the lobby exactly would have made every visit to a casting page fire that off. So the boxes now load when you open them and not before. You would not see any difference except a normal moment's loading the first time you open billing in a session. The underlying sloppiness is filed as its own job (#306) rather than spread around.

THE QUEUE: 90 open, 13 urgent, 9 waiting on you, and nothing rotting — no card has sat untouched for a week. Next up is #301, a privacy check that stops one of your Casts from deleting, which is a live bug on your own account.

SATURDAY'S APPROVAL IS BUILT — AND THE REASON IT TOOK FOUR NIGHTS IS THE MORE USEFUL HALF.

You approved the component move at 3:39 on Saturday morning: five shared parts out of casting and into the shared kit, the stylesheet renamed first, the three dialogs built on one shell. It did not get built. Three shifts in a row read a handoff note saying "do NOT move components on #262" and stood down — and that note was written an HOUR BEFORE you said yes. Each shift copied it forward without opening the card. Tonight's shift opened the card, found your approval at the top of it, and built it.

WHAT YOU WOULD NOTICE: nothing, and that is the acceptance test. Same dialogs, same rename box at its deliberately lighter 428px, same overflow menu. I opened all of it in the running app in both light and dark before it shipped.

You cleared your whole desk tonight - ten replies in about half an hour, across six cards. Every one of them is now written against its issue in your own words, so none of it lives only in a message. Nothing new was built after the first piece of work; the rest of the shift was making sure your answers landed somewhere they survive.

On the reader court: you were right and I was wrong, and the mistake is worth naming because it is a specific one rather than bad luck. The Grok arm was timing out at 45 seconds, and I let those cells count as refusals - so a slow reader got scored as a bad one, and my write-up said Grok refused the creature when Grok never answered at all. That last clause is the opposite of what our region reader does - it never writes neither, it always draws something - which is the fault you ruled to N3 twenty minutes earlier. Two answers of yours pointing the same way in the same half hour.

The hero is marked done on your word. The spec toggle stays open on its own card so it does not vanish behind the green tick.

Nothing else was started tonight. The species-rule sentence, the bug-report reader, the MAX author fixes and the Grok bench are four separate shifts' work and they are all specified now, so the next shifts can pick them up without asking you anything.

Last note - two more from you after the previous one went out.

On the lookalike reader: yes, exactly as you said, and it was already done before your message arrived - the note is in the plan at N3 with the measurements and the list of places it actually affects.

On the species rule: your sentence and your four checks are written down on the card word for word, and nothing has been started. That is deliberate. It changes the house block, which goes into every cast on the author road, and it needs four paid renders to check - so it is a whole shift rather than the last twenty minutes of one, and your own line gave the pause. The live behaviour is untouched tonight, as you asked.

I have set your two rollback conditions up as two separate tests rather than one score, because they guard different things: the goth growing fangs condemns the sentence, and the lamia losing her coils condemns it too, but for the opposite reason. Rolled into one verdict you would not be able to see which happened.

And you have now told us three times in three replies not to trust the pixel tool. It is written into the brief as the method rather than as a note - the four checks get judged by eye. You are right about that instrument specifically, which is the part I would not have wanted you to have to say twice: the thing that counted horns as tusks is the same reader you ruled to N3 half an hour earlier.

Second note tonight, because six replies from you landed while I was working and two of them ruled the exact thing I was working on. All six are now recorded against their cards, in your words, so none of them lives only in a message.

On the lookalike reader: you said add a note to N3 and fix it at that milestone. Done, and the note carries what tonight's work found so nobody has to re-derive it. The short version is that the faulty answer is used in 28 places in the studio, 16 of them switched on, and the widest one is the face panel - on every account, drawing a rectangle whenever the reader finds any pixels at all, with no minimum. Two of the words I have measured this fault on are panel words, and a third panel word is horns, which is the floating rectangle you reported yourself. So it belongs exactly where you put it.

I have flagged one thing in the plan as NOT covered by N3, so finishing that rung is never read as finishing this: the refund decision on a paid removal reads the same reader. If it draws the thing back onto a picture we correctly cleaned, we call our own render a failure and refund. Your money is safe; the customer loses the picture. That is an editing-road fix, not a panel fix.

Your question about the two faces was the best thing that happened tonight, and I want to say why. You asked whether the left one was horns and the right one tusks. Both right - I opened them full size to check rather than answering from the numbers. But the right-hand face has BOTH horns and tusks in shot, and asked for tusks it picked the tusks and left the horns alone. So the reader is not muddling the two words; it knows them apart perfectly well when both are there. It only invents when the real thing is missing. Three sittings of measuring had not made that distinction, and it kills the cheapest theory - that the words are too alike and need separating - before anyone spends a night on it.

Your other three: the creature lane is filed as an order to ship, with your two "don't trust the pixel counter" sentences kept verbatim because you said it twice and that makes it the point rather than an aside. Bug reports - option D, admin panel first, and I have written down that you said FIRST and not ONLY so nobody builds it in a way that makes adding the moderator view later a rewrite. The MAX author - (a) and (c) are go, and (b) is written down with your condition attached rather than as a maybe, because your bar is a real one: a measured test showing a specific phrase blocks a GOOD draft, not a clumsy first one.

None of those three were built tonight. They arrived mid-shift and they are somebody's whole brief each, so they are filed as instructions for the next shift rather than half-started.

Short version: the measuring fault you have been shown two nights running is not a laboratory curiosity. It is wired into 28 places in the studio, 16 of them switched on right now, and one of those is on every account. No new measurement tonight and no money spent - this was the question your own card asked first and nobody had done: where does that answer actually get used?

The answer that matters most is the face panel. When you open a cast, the studio draws a small rectangle on each feature it finds, and the rule for drawing one is "the reader found some pixels" - any pixels, no minimum. That rule was written down deliberately, with a reason attached: anatomy like eyes and hair was assumed not to need a minimum, because anatomy would surely answer honestly about whether it is there. That is precisely the assumption the last two nights disproved. Both words I have measured the fault on are panel words. So is horns - the floating rectangle you reported yourself months ago.

And those rectangles are not decoration. Clicking one opens a prefilled edit box that spends credits at the normal price. The panel's own code says the promise out loud: a rectangle over the wrong pixels is a promise that clicking there edits that thing.

The second place is the refund decision on removals. If the reader draws the thing back onto a picture the studio correctly cleaned, the studio decides its own render failed and refunds. Your money is safe either way - what the customer loses is the picture she paid for and which was right.

Two more places mint things that are kept forever - the tattoo crop and the feature library - so a wrong outline there gets carried into every later edit rather than being a one-off.

One piece of genuinely good news, because it deserves saying plainly: both safety reads on the tattoo-upload road fail the SAFE way. A mistake there makes the studio more careful, never less. Nothing about a customer's photograph is loosened by any of this.

Nothing was repaired tonight. Your open choice on this is still open, and I have not touched it - but it now has an address, which it did not have this morning, and my recommendation to you is on the card: fix the panel first, because it is the widest and the cheapest, then measure the remaining nine words before anyone goes near the refund path.

Worth admitting: the tool I wrote to do this census got it wrong on the first pass. It went looking for the flag and missed two whole parts of the studio that genuinely call the reader - one because the call is written ten lines below its own argument, one because the flag arrives as a parameter instead of being typed out. That is the exact mistake this project has a law about, turning up inside the instrument built to survey it. It is anchored on the call now, and it refuses to run at all unless every mention in the server is accounted for.

Short version: the measuring fault you were shown last night is now confirmed in a second, independent place - and the fix I recommended to you would not have caught either of them. That second part is the important bit, and it is why tonight was worth doing.

Recap in one line. When the studio takes something OFF a face - shave the head, take the earrings out - it re-reads the picture afterwards to check its own work. Last night I showed you that this checker, asked "where is the hair" of a completely bald head, drew a hair-shaped cap on the bare skin instead of saying "there is none". It ended with a question for you, because I had got a similar call wrong earlier that same night and your eye is the one that counts.

Tonight I did the thing that means you no longer have to answer that question for us to know where we stand: I tested a completely different word, on completely different faces. The word is eyebrows - an ordinary thing a customer asks to remove, unlike the creature words we had been using.

It happened again, twice in four tries. On a creature with no eyebrow hair at all, the checker painted two perfect eyebrow shapes onto the bare ridge above its eyes. There is a picture on your page and it needs no explaining.

And here is the number that made me stop. That invented pair measured BIGGER than the real eyebrows on the two ordinary faces I checked alongside it - bigger than a woman's dark brows, bigger than a man's blond ones. So we cannot tell a real feature from an invented one by size: the invented one wins.

Both the checks I ran the other way held, which is what makes this evidence rather than noise. A blank grey picture through the same code correctly said "nothing there", and both faces that DO have eyebrows came back correctly on their real eyebrows. The tool is good at this word when the word has something to point at. It just does not know how to say no.

Now the part that changes your decision. I recommended a fix to you: make each feature's answer land in the part of the face that feature lives in - a mouth thing near the mouth. Free, simple, and it works on the case we first found. I put both nights' answers side by side and it does not work here. The invented eyebrows sit in exactly the same strip of the picture as real eyebrows - identical, to the digit. The invented hair sat inside the strip real hair occupies.

There is a reason, and it is the kind that generalises. This particular check only ever looks at a face we JUST removed something from. What a removal leaves behind is the thing the feature was sitting on - the ridge under the eyebrows, the scalp under the hair, the jaw under a beard, the earlobe under an earring. A feature and the thing it sits on are in the same place by definition, so a rule about WHERE an answer sits can never separate them.

So I have changed my recommendation on your card, and the reason is on it. The free positional fix stays right for the place we originally found this; for this particular check it would leave us exactly as wrong as we are now while looking fixed - which is worse than knowing, because a fix with a name stops anyone looking again.

Nobody is affected today. I checked the live records again: this step has still never run for a customer. That is the third night running where the fault is real and the customer count is zero, and it is the argument for doing it before the editing work starts rather than after.

Tonight cost six and a half cents of house money in thirteen picture readings. No credits, no renders, nothing on production touched but this briefing and one picture uploaded for it. Your Fable review allowance is still out - my own pull request tonight got the same one-second empty refusal - so this was another measurement-and-record night by the team's own rule.

One last thing, because it is the system working rather than a problem. The gate rejected my own change tonight - I had tinted a caption pink on one of these pictures, and there is a standing rule of yours that anything drawn on top of a photograph is white or grey, never coloured. It was right to stop me. When I went to fix it I found the rule's checker only recognises two of the three ways this codebase writes a colour, so it had waved through the actual overlay three lines away and caught only the caption. The overlays are white now, which is what your rule asks for, and the pictures on this page were repainted from the readings already taken rather than re-bought - each one checked against its recorded number so the picture still shows the reading underneath it. The checker's blind spot is written up as its own card rather than quietly patched by me at three in the morning.

A correction, to something I put on your problems board an hour ago and to what the two shifts before me had written there.

We have been telling you that the text account's balance "has not moved for a third night running". That is wrong, and it is wrong in the direction that matters: it makes the account look frozen and the spending look like zero.

What actually happened is that the shifts run back to back through one night, a few minutes apart, and each of us called our own reading "tonight" and the previous one "last night". Three readings taken within about two hours became, in the writing, three days of a stuck number.

The real picture, read off the deploy receipts rather than off memory: on 29 August the balance went from $9.79 in the morning to $7.70 by evening, and $7.70 is genuinely where it has sat - for one hour and forty-nine minutes, across four deploys. The account's own counter says $3.59 was spent that day. So it is spending normally; nothing is stuck.

The runway estimate you were given - about two days - was right all along. It was only the story around it that drifted.

One thing I checked while I was there, because it kills a possibility rather than raising one: the key we use and the account are the same thing. The key's lifetime spend and the account's spent figure are the identical number to eight decimal places, so there is no second key quietly draining it. What remains true is the original point: money goes out and the granted figure has not gone up since 27 August.

Tonight I found a door in the product that opens onto nothing, and I have left it for you rather than fixing it, because the fix is a decision about privacy and that is yours.

In the lobby there is a quiet three-dot menu with two entries: Send feedback, and Report a bug. Any approved customer can type out what went wrong, press send, and gets back "Bug report submitted. Thank you!" It is stored in the database. And that is the end of it. There is no page anywhere in the product - not for you, not for an admin, not for a moderator - that can read it back. I swept all 950 source files: the table is written and never read. The second half of the road was a Slack message, and there is no Slack webhook configured on production at all, so that message becomes a log line that is wiped on the next deploy.

So a customer's report reaches nobody. Nobody has been failed yet - the table holds zero rows, all time - but the button is live for every approved account on a desktop, so that is luck rather than design.

I checked how it got this way rather than guessing, because "never finished" and "broken by a later change" point at different repairs. Nothing was lost: a reader has never existed in this repository's history, on any branch. The Slack notification WAS meant to be the reader, and production has never had Slack.

I then swept every other table for the same shape - written by the product, read by nothing. There are four, and three of them are correct as they stand: they are counting tallies whose whole design is that a person reads them by hand when a decision comes up, and they deliberately hold no names, no sentences and no pictures. The fourth is this one, and it is the only one that holds a person's own words.

Why I stopped rather than building it: the project's own access rules name bug reports specifically, and say staff get none by default and anything wider is a deliberate exception. Putting a customer's typed complaint in front of a moderator IS that exception. There is a card on your desk with four ways to fix it. My recommendation is the smallest one: email you when a report arrives, using the email system that already sends verification mail. That needs no new page and no rule change, and the report reaches a human in seconds.

The rest of the night was reading. Nothing was spent - no renders, no credits, no engine calls of any kind.

Tonight I fixed something the studio was saying to customers that was simply not true, and it was about to start saying it to everyone.

When our reader - the thing that turns your typed words into an edit - fails to answer, the studio used to reply: "That one didn't come through clearly. Try naming what you want changed about them." In other words, it blamed the customer's sentence. Two other places did the same with photographs: "We couldn't read that picture - try another one." None of that is true when the failure is ours. She rewrites her sentence, it fails again. She uploads a different photo, it fails again. The studio blames her every single time, and she has no way of knowing it was never her.

Casting a whole brief already got this right - that was your "refuse-free" ruling back in August, which made a failed read refuse for free AND say plainly that our reader did not answer. What I found is that the ruling's second half - say it was ours - only ever reached the casting page. The three editing roads got the free part and kept the old sentence. The reason nobody spotted it is quite reassuring: the sweep that went looking after your ruling asked "is anyone being charged for this?", and the answer was no, correctly, everywhere. The money was right, so nobody read the words.

Why tonight: our text account (OpenRouter - the one that reads every brief and every edit) is down to $7.70, about two days. At zero this stops being a rare glitch and becomes what EVERY customer sees on EVERY edit. I did not want that sentence to be the one they got.

One more thing worth telling you, because three of my own shift reports had been repeating it without ever checking: the claim that "at zero, nothing gets charged" is now proven rather than assumed. I drove both paid roads with a fake engine that fails exactly the way an empty account fails. Both refuse before any money moves. No credits, no renders, nothing deducted. That part of the product does the right thing and now there is evidence for it.

Nothing about pricing, refunds or what the studio can do has changed. It is the same refusal - it just tells the truth about whose fault it was.

Nothing in the studio changed tonight - no product code at all - and one new thing needs your call.

The brief was a small defect filed last night: the writer that turns your words into a richer paragraph on MAX occasionally slips a note about its own job into the picture instructions. The card said the cheap way to measure it was to read our records. I tried that first, and the useful finding is that it does not work - the studio has recorded five of those paragraphs in its entire life, because MAX is your setting alone and LOW uses no writer. So I bought a measurement instead: 24 runs on three of your own briefs, 26 cents.

It happens about one time in six, and the assumption behind the card was backwards. We thought the writer does it when told not to add things to a rich brief. It is the opposite - it does it most on THIN briefs, where it starts narrating what it is leaving open. One draft told the image engine that jewellery was "left to the engine". I did not fix it, because I also measured that the obvious fix does not work: the phrase that looks most like the tell is your own legitimate wording four times out of five, and my deliberately over-wide detector still missed one of the four real cases.

The bigger thing came out of the same 24 runs and it is on your desk as a card. Our own safety rules refuse the writer's first draft more than half the time, and one time in five they refuse it twice - at which point the studio quietly sends your raw words instead, exactly as if the meter were on LOW, while the sheet still says Max. The cause is two of our own good rules getting in each other's way: the writer reaching for skin words the realism block bans, and the writer saying "youthful" about a brief that says mid 30s. Both rules are right on their own terms.

My recommendation is the small honest one first - tell the customer when the writer sat it out, using a sentence we have already written for a neighbouring case - and leave the rules alone until there is a proper before/after test. The rest is on the card.

Still waiting on you for the lobby lane: nothing gets built there until you name which segment is first.

Nothing in the studio changed tonight and nothing new needs you. Team tooling again - and it closes out the job the last two shifts were working on.

The short version: the automatic test run that guards every change has been going red on a different check each time whenever your computer was busy. Last night's shift fixed the biggest offender. Tonight's shift asked whether the rest of it needed fixing too, measured it properly, and found the answer was NOT the obvious one.

The obvious answer is 'give everything more time'. The measurement said no. The same ten thousand checks were run twice - once quiet, once with the machine deliberately loaded up the way it is when you are using it - and paired one by one. Nine thousand nine hundred and fifty of them finished in under a second either way. Exactly ONE ran out of time. Loosening the limit for all ten thousand, to rescue one, would have made the run worse at spotting a check that is genuinely stuck - which is the whole point of having a limit.

So the eight checks that genuinely need longer were given longer, and every one of them earned it by having actually failed before, not by looking slow on a stopwatch. That distinction turned out to matter: the check that DID fail had looked perfectly comfortable when the machine was quiet, and the one that looked closest to the edge got faster under load.

Two things worth flagging, both found by the work rather than assumed.

First, the run taken to prove the fix had worked killed a check that ALREADY had extra time and had quietly grown into it - it used 100% of its allowance. So the real question is not which checks are slow, it is which ones are close to their own ceiling. Two were, and both are now fixed.

Second, a housekeeping mistake worth knowing about because it hides work rather than breaking it. Last night's shift closed its task with a note saying the job was only half done and the card must stay open - but the way the note was written, the system closed the card anyway, about ninety seconds before that very sentence was posted. The next shift then read the queue, could not see it, and would never have found the other half. I only found it by opening it directly. The card was reopened, the second half is now done, and I checked the last twenty-five merges for the same mistake - it had happened only this once.

Nothing in the studio changed tonight and nothing new needs you. This was the team's own tooling, and it finishes the job the last shift deliberately left half done.

Every change we make has to pass a set of automatic checks first. One of them was taking two minutes of solid work on its own, which made the whole run go red whenever your machine was busy - a red that looks exactly like a real failure. Last night's shift found the cause: the check was repeating the same expensive piece of work twenty-two times over an unchanged tree. It also found something more uncomfortable, and stopped: the obvious, faster fix silently switches OFF the very safety check it lives inside, and when it does, the test results look identical to a working one.

Tonight the safe version shipped. It is now 29 seconds instead of 119, and the full run of all 10,307 tests takes 83 seconds.

But the reason I am telling you about it is the bit underneath. That check works by building the studio's map twice and comparing the two. Nothing had ever tested that the COMPARISON itself works - every test fed it a map that was correct, so they all agreed it was correct, and not one of them could have noticed the comparison being deleted. I proved that rather than assumed it: I broke it on purpose, two different ways, and all eighteen existing tests stayed green both times.

So the speed-up had to buy a new guard before it was allowed in - one that hands the check a deliberately broken map and insists it complains, and which goes red the moment anyone takes the tempting shortcut. That guard is now in, and it has been seen to fail, which is the only way to know a guard works.

Two honest notes. The review robot on our pull requests is still down - your Fable allowance has been exhausted for about 31 hours - so nothing external read this change. What stood in its place is that it carries its own proof: the broken-on-purpose test. And the money line is unchanged and still worth a glance when you are back: the OpenRouter balance is $8.05 and its top-up has not landed in five days.

Still waiting on you, and not started: which lobby segment you want first, and the bald-skull question from two nights ago.

A quiet, useful night on the team's own tools - nothing in the studio changed, and nothing new needs you.

Before any change the team makes can go anywhere, it has to pass a set of automatic checks. One of those checks has been failing for the wrong reason: not because anything is broken, but because it runs out of time when your computer is doing something else. Two earlier shifts hit it, wrote it down carefully, and deliberately did NOT fix it - their reasoning was good and I want to repeat it, because it is the right instinct: raising a time limit without knowing why something is slow is how a slow tool becomes permanent. So they left the question open. Tonight I answered it.

The check builds a complete picture of the codebase and compares it against the one we have on file. It turns out it builds that picture from scratch twenty-two times in a row, from files that have not changed between one build and the next, and about eighty-three per cent of each build is one expensive step being repeated for nothing. That is where the two minutes goes - not growth, just the same work over and over.

I measured the repair rather than proposing it. Reusing that one expensive step takes the check from a hundred and nineteen seconds to nineteen, with all seventeen of its own tests still passing. Six times faster.

But here is the part worth your attention, and it is the reason I think tonight was worth a night. There is an even faster version - seven seconds - and it is the one anybody would reach for first, including me. I tested it by deliberately breaking the underlying tool and watching whether the check would notice. The nineteen-second version caught it and said so by name. The seven-second version said nothing at all: it had quietly switched off one of the safety checks inside itself, and reported everything as fine over a genuinely broken tool. It would have shipped looking like the bigger win, and we would have had a smoke alarm with the battery taken out.

That is measured rather than argued - I ran the real check four times, breaking one thing at a time, and it put itself back each time.

I did not ship any of it. The file involved sits on the path every single change travels through, and your Fable reviewer is still out - twenty-fourth refusal, about thirty hours now, well past the only precedent we have. So this is a sixth night of the team's own rule: measurements, tooling and written records may go ahead; anything touching money or the product waits for you. It is written up and queued with the numbers attached, so whoever picks it up is choosing between measured options instead of guessing.

Cost: nothing at all. No credits, no renders, no picture readings, no house money - tonight was reading code and running our own tests. Nothing on production was touched but this briefing.

Still waiting on you, unchanged from last night: which lobby segment you want first, and whether that left-hand skull in last night's picture reads as bald to you.
